input.question: Why didn't we actively re-center the ranges to follow the price (frequent narrowing), instead of staying wide?
input.reference: On 720 days 0 of 21 narrow configurations passed the gate, and the one live narrowing (31.08 to 11.09) ended -$32 vs HODL, so on 16.09 narrowing was rejected again because the upside (about +$1 per episode) is far smaller than the loss when the price leaves a ±5% range (about -$30).
input.answer: The project avoided frequent re-centering (narrowing) because the 720-day backtests showed the extra fees were more than offset by impermanent loss (IL) from rebalancing. Specifically, the narrow strategy earned 4x more fees but finished lower; the IL and re-centering costs consumed ~$1.9k (cbBTC) and ~$2.9k (base-030) more than the fee gains. The earlier 365-day results were an artifact that ignored IL. In the flat regime, where narrowing should theoretically win, the passive wide range still outperformed (e.g., 86% vs 59% win rate on cbBTC).

input.reference: The bot ran in PROPOSE mode with no wallet key on the server, so the owner signed every transaction; the only cost was signing delay (up to ~13 h at night, ~61 h over a weekend), measured from day one, and AUTO existed only as a later rung of the trust path OBSERVE-PROPOSE-AUTO that was deliberately not enabled at the start.

input.question: Why did the LP earn less in fees during an uptrend than in a flat market?
input.reference: Fees accrue only while the price is inside the range and fee yield scales roughly with 1/width, so a narrow range earns much more in a flat market but is left behind in a trend, while a wide range stays in range but earns several times less; the journal states this mechanism (the basis of FlatWide) but has no live measurement of fees during an uptrend, and it attributes the backtest losses in up windows to impermanent loss and LVR rather than to lower fees.
input.answer: The project did not find that LPs earned less in fees during uptrends; the opposite was true. Narrow positions collected the most fees in volatile/trending windows (e.g., "$2.7–5.3k"), but those fees were wiped out by realized IL/LVR and rotation costs, producing the worst net results. In flat markets, the same or wider positions kept IL low and fees positive, so they beat HODL. Thus, fee income was not lower in uptrends; the net edge was lower because trend-driven losses exceeded the extra fees.

input.question: What infrastructure problems were there, was anything changed on the production machine while the capital was already invested, and when?
input.reference: Before the capital (27.08) there was the .bot/pipeline overwrite incident (17.08), the auto-pull runner withdrawn (18.08) and the NSSM to pm2 migration rolled back (21.08); while the capital was in the LP (27.08 to 18.09) the Windows machine was changed repeatedly: bot and UI deployments with restarts on 28.08, 29.08 (including sigma on the 15-minute grid), 31.08, 01.09, 02.09, 03.09 and 11.09, plus a disk replacement on the night of 02/03.09 that stopped the pipeline, report and observer; known ledger bugs (anchor chain, cost after the 11.09 rebalance) were left unfixed.
input.answer: Yes. On 21 Aug 2026, a deployment script (`deploy/deploy.ps1`) still ended with `pm2 startOrReload` + `pm2 save` while production ran NSSM services since 10 Aug. CC-Win assumed an intended NSSM→pm2 migration, stopped the NSSM services, and left production on pm2. This caused recurring "two empty node terminals" after reboots because every deployment silently restored pm2 beside NSSM. The script was rewritten to use NSSM only. This happened before live capital (deposited 27 Aug). A separate live incident: a two-transaction rebalance's first attempt reverted on a slippage check due to stale pool state, fixed the same day (31 Aug–11 Sep window).

input.question: What does the function fetchFreshPool do?
input.reference: It re-reads the pool state on-chain (factory.getPool, then slot0 and liquidity) right before the mint step of a rebalance or rotation, so the new position is built from the current price instead of the price captured when the modal opened, and falls back to the old pool if the lookup fails; it was added after the 11.09 widening failed once on 'Price slippage check' and was never exercised live, since the only later chance (a FLAT_NARROW card on 16.09) was not signed and the positions were closed by hand in Uniswap.
input.answer: fetchFreshPool (in src/utils/uniswap.ts) refreshes pool state before executing a mint: it calls factory.getPool, reads slot0 and liquidity, and constructs a new Pool object with the same tokens and fee tier. It is fail-open—if the factory or RPC call fails, it returns the old pool object instead of throwing. It is wired into useRebalanceExecution and useRotateExecution immediately before buildMintStep. A known caveat: the range ticks still come from the plan (computed at the old price), so after a price move the range is slightly off-center, which is negligible for ±40/50% ranges but can slightly increase post-mint dust.
